title: Game Mathematics Part 2: Quaternions 1 — From Imaginary Numbers to Rotation and Inverses

scenes.title: 두 편의 지도와 첫 편의 질문
lines: This quaternion lecture has two episodes. After outlining the complete journey, this first episode explains how to construct a stored rotation and undo it.

scenes.title: 이번 강의에서 배울 것
lines: How can four numbers record an airborne rotation in a game?
We will observe ski and bike orientations, then visualize the four quaternion components and their half-angle.
We will undo and compose rotations, and compute the difference between two orientations.
Finally, we will check sign and normalization pitfalls and rotate a vector in a worked exercise.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Our goal is to record the body's orientation at one instant. Let us first distinguish where the rider is from how the body is turned.

scenes.title: 스키의 이동과 자세를 나누어 보기
lines: This is skiing in Riders Republic. Watch the tilt of the body and skis.
Read forward movement separately from changes in body orientation.
In the air, the travel path continues while facing and bank also change.
Remaining near screen center does not imply an unchanged orientation; the camera follows too.
We are learning a representation that can describe the visible motion, without claiming to have inspected the game code.
Our next diagram will hold position fixed and rotate the three body axes to isolate orientation.

scenes.title: 허수는 왜 등장할까?
lines: To understand this approach to rotation through multiplication, we first extend the number system. The square of a real number is nonnegative, so no real number squares to minus one.
We define a new rule in which i squared is minus one. The number i defined this way is called the imaginary unit.
This rule does not make an imaginary number a hidden object inside the game. It provides a useful numerical tool for direction calculations.
To see why it helps with rotation, we will represent these numbers as point coordinates.

scenes.title: 아이를 곱하면 왜 90도 돌아갈까?
lines: A complex number a+bi represents a point (a,b) in a plane. Its horizontal coordinate is the real part and its vertical coordinate is the coefficient of i.
The point with x coordinate two and y coordinate one is 2+i. Multiplying by i gives 2i+i squared, which equals minus one plus 2i.
The new x coordinate is minus one and the new y coordinate is two. The arrow turns ninety degrees counterclockwise while retaining length square root of five.
Multiplying a point (a,b) by i changes it to (-b,a), allowing multiplication to represent a planar turn.
In three dimensions, we also need an axis that defines the rotation plane. We will extend this direction calculation to a quaternion using that axis.

scenes.title: 구십 도에서 다른 각도로 넓히기
lines: We verified that multiplying by i produces a ninety-degree turn. How can we represent other angles?
Recall the unit circle from high-school trigonometry. A unit arrow turned by theta has horizontal component cos(theta) and vertical component sin(theta).
Multiplication by cos(theta)+i sin(theta) therefore rotates the plane by theta. At ninety degrees the cosine is zero and the sine is one, giving i.
This planar calculation uses the full physical angle theta. When the three-dimensional quaternion later uses a half-angle, we will compare the different operation applied to the vector.

scenes.title: 평면의 회전에서 삼차원 축으로
lines: We learned about a planar angle.
Observe the red torso line.
Three dimensions require an axis too.
We now connect it to the three axis components.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: In a plane, two numbers and multiplication could turn a direction. Extending that idea to three dimensions requires choosing an axis; let us examine the numbers we need.

scenes.title: 네 숫자는 세 축과 어떤 관계일까?
lines: A scalar means one number. Here a vector is a three-number group describing a direction, and a component is an individual number in that group.
The symbols i,j,k belong to the three-dimensional rotation algebra. We do not need to draw a fourth physical direction to store four numbers.
For a z-axis rotation, x and y are zero while w and z carry angle information. These are not four independent rotation angles.
Which values produce 90 degrees? We will construct them using a unit axis and familiar trigonometry.

scenes.title: 네 성분은 네 회전 각도가 아니다
lines: A quaternion contains one scalar and a three-component vector. We write components in w,x,y,z order.
A unit rotation quaternion has squared components summing to one, leaving three continuous degrees of freedom.
Four numbers are not four rotation angles, and x,y,z are not Euler angles.
The algebra uses i,j,k, whose squares each equal minus one.
The product ij is k, whereas ji is minus k: an early hint that order matters.
A library may store x,y,z,w instead. Check the named components and memory order.

scenes.title: 숫자 세 개가 담는 방향을 날개로 관찰하기
lines: Read the direction represented by three components through the wings. This excerpt changes from bicycle travel to flight.
The red line joins the visible wing tips. Compare it with the teal screen-horizontal reference.
The camera also moves, so this projected angle is not a world rotation angle.
How do we construct four components from an axis and angle independent of the camera?

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We have separated the roles of the four components. Now we need to construct them from the axis and angle introduced in the preceding lesson.

scenes.title: 축·각에서 반각으로 연결하기
lines: Recall a unit axis and the angle of rotation about it.
The scalar is cos of the half-angle, and the vector is the unit axis times sin of the half-angle.
At zero angle, cos is one and sin is zero, giving the identity [1,0,0,0].
A 90-degree z rotation uses a 45-degree half-angle, so w and z are both sqrt(2)/2.
The half-angle does not mean half the physical rotation. Multiplication on both sides produces the full angle.
We retain right-handed column-vector conventions, and use radians in trigonometric calculations.

scenes.title: 반각으로 저장해도 회전은 90도
lines: A planar rotation used sine and cosine of the full angle, but our quaternion uses 45 degrees for a 90-degree turn. This needs an explanation.
The difference is how we later apply it: the rotation value multiplies the vector on the left, and its inverse multiplies it on the right.
The complete two-sided operation produces the 90-degree z rotation. A one-sided intermediate is not a physical 45-degree orientation of the object.
For now, distinguish the stored half-angle from the physical turn; we will later calculate both products on the same vector to verify the connection.

scenes.title: 반각은 화면에서 절반만 도는 뜻이 아니다
lines: The half-angle belonged to the storage formula. Observe the red torso and blue wheel lines.
The complete two-sided operation produces ninety degrees; it does not rotate the object by half.
We now connect the four components to the visible orientation.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We have defined a 90-degree turn about z. Returning to the game, we can watch body directions change together; the angle projected by a moving camera is not our defined world angle.

scenes.title: 몸에 붙인 축과 공중 회전
lines: Compare body facing when the skis leave the ground and when they land.
Imagine three small body axes; all of them rotate together in the air.
One direction alone cannot describe both body facing and ski bank.
A quaternion is one way to store the full orientation, not position or velocity.
We are not measuring exact axes and angles from the screen. We will define those explicitly in the next calculation.
Watch orientation separately from travel direction around landing to connect the representation to visible motion.

scenes.title: 한 번의 변화에서 두 번의 연산으로
lines: An axis and angle gave us a rotation value. Observe the red torso and blue wheel lines.
What happens when we apply that rotation twice about one axis?
We now compose two ninety-degree turns into one product.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We saw the whole orientation change. What happens if we apply the same 90-degree turn again? We will calculate a fixed-axis example rather than measure a particular game maneuver.

scenes.title: 구십 도 회전을 두 번 합치면
lines: Multiply the z90 quaternion by itself, applying the same rotation twice.
The new scalar is the product of scalars minus the vector dot product, which is zero here.
The two cross scalar-vector terms sum to a z component of one; the other components remain zero.
The result [0,0,0,1] represents z180.
After two more such rotations, the result is [-1,0,0,0], with the body back at its initial orientation.
The scalar changed from one to minus one, yet the orientation matches. Let us examine this double representation.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Four turns restored the orientation but changed the signs of its stored components. We must explain that difference to compare orientations correctly.

scenes.title: q와 -q는 같은 자세
lines: The unit quaternions q and -q produce the same rotation matrix and endpoint orientation.
All four components change sign. This differs from conjugation, which changes only the vector signs.
In vector rotation, the signs on both sides cancel.
Component equality alone is therefore insufficient to test orientation equality.
Equivalent endpoints do not make every interpolation path between signed representatives equivalent.
Endpoint orientation does not retain revolution count; store the path and accumulated rotation separately.

scenes.title: 같은 끝 자세와 지나온 회전 과정을 구분하기
lines: The equality of q and minus q concerned the ending orientation. Continue observing the jump and landing.
The red torso line and blue ski line record visible directions over time.
One endpoint image cannot recover the intervening turn.
Our calculation flips all components; it does not reverse rotation or rewind a route.
Which value applies no extra rotation? We verify the same input in the following explanation.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Different component signs represented the same final orientation.
Can that orientation reveal the preceding motion?
Let us follow one interval through time.

scenes.title: 같은 자세로 돌아와도 움직임은 남는다
lines: Follow the body forward direction and ski line through the airborne rotation.
A single frame cannot reveal the full movement that preceded it.
Time reveals the process; endpoint orientation and movement history are different information.
Connect this distinction to the two signed quaternions representing one orientation.
One quaternion does not automatically retain the number of visible revolutions.
If a trick needs accumulated rotation, track input or rotation history separately from orientation.

scenes.title: 변화가 없다는 연산도 입력과 결과로 읽기
lines: An endpoint pose did not store every earlier action.
Observe the torso and wheels during snow travel.
The red line shows the torso direction.
The blue line shows a visible wheel direction.
Both directions change through slopes and bends.
Identity rotation does not mean that the whole game image stops.
It applies no extra rotation to an input direction.
Treat the torso direction as the input.
Which four components return it unchanged?

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Final orientation and rotation history are different information. We now need a value that adds no rotation, and will check why initializing every component to zero fails.

scenes.title: 항등원과 부호를 구분하기
lines: The multiplication identity is [1,0,0,0]; multiplying q by it leaves q unchanged.
[-1,0,0,0] is also the identity rotation, but is not the algebraic multiplication identity.
It changes q to -q: different components representing the same orientation.
An all-zero quaternion is not no rotation; it is a zero-norm invalid rotation input.
Initialize with the library identity constructor or correctly ordered unit components.
Distinguish equality as numbers from equality as rotations before reasoning about signs.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: The identity value had length one. Other stored rotations use that same convention, so we need to detect drift caused by repeated calculations.

scenes.title: 길이와 정규화의 조건
lines: The norm is the square root of the sum of all four squared components, not just the vector norm.
Typical orientation storage and quaternion-to-matrix routines expect unit inputs.
For small floating-point drift, divide all four components by the norm.
Guard near-zero and nonfinite norms before division; do not disguise arbitrary invalid data as a valid rotation.
A nonzero nonunit quaternion can also rotate with its correct general inverse because scale cancels, unlike unit-assuming code.
Normalization restores the scale convention. It neither scales the rotation angle directly nor fixes wrong axes or multiplication order.

scenes.title: 정규화는 방향을 고치는 일이 아니다
lines: Normalization means changing the norm to one. For [3,0,0,4], the norm is the square root of three squared plus four squared, which is five.
Divide all four components by five. The scalar becomes 0.6, both x and y remain zero, and z becomes 0.8. The squared norm is 0.36 plus 0.64, which equals one.
The numerical magnitude changes while the axis and component ratios remain. This does not correct a wrongly selected axis or multiplication order.
Likewise, faster character motion does not require a larger orientation quaternion norm. We will observe speed and orientation separately in the game.

scenes.title: 속도 숫자와 자세값의 길이를 나누기
lines: The rotation quaternion had norm one. Separate the displayed speed from the visible body direction.
This is a separate flight excerpt. The red wing line shows orientation; the moving position shows a route.
A larger speed display does not imply a larger unit-rotation norm.
Next, the equipment changes to a bicycle. Apparent size and speed differ, while the unit-length condition remains the same.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We have checked normalization. To avoid thinking that faster movement needs a longer quaternion, we will observe speed and orientation separately.

scenes.title: 속도 변화와 자세 저장값
lines: We will move from skiing to a flight segment. Watch movement speed separately from body orientation.
Faster motion does not mean a longer quaternion; a unit rotation retains norm one.
Speed and acceleration describe change, whereas orientation describes the current state.
The following camera moves as the wings bank. Apparent image size cannot reveal quaternion norm.
Check unit length in code or data; this footage is not a measurement of those values.
After observing motion, we will calculate how to undo a stored rotation in the next diagram.

scenes.title: 기울기를 상쇄할 때 남는 이동
lines: Riding and flight are separate excerpts. Read speed and orientation separately.
During flight, read the red wing tilt separately from the speed display.
Which components change to undo our unit rotation? We now calculate with the conjugate.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Orientation and speed were separate quantities. Let us now undo a stored rotation; the unit-length condition we maintained makes this calculation simpler.

scenes.title: 켤레로 단위 회전을 되돌리기
lines: Conjugation keeps the scalar and negates the three vector components.
For a unit rotation quaternion, the conjugate is the inverse and undoes the rotation.
Conjugating z90 preserves w and negates z, giving z minus90.
Their product returns [1,0,0,0].
Negating all four components instead gives the same orientation, not generally the inverse.
Special cases such as half-turns have matching inverse orientations, but conjugation and full negation remain different operations.

scenes.title: 역회전은 주행 경로의 되감기가 아니다
lines: We inverted a unit rotation with its conjugate. Separate the red torso line from the traveled position.
Even as the bank becomes smaller, the bicycle continues forward. Rotation and translation are different changes.
An inverse cancels the defined rotation. It does not rewind elapsed time or distance.
Would conjugation alone invert a tuple whose norm is not one? We verify that condition next.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Conjugation undid a unit quaternion. Does the same formula work when its length is not one? A small numerical example will check whether their product is the identity.

scenes.title: 일반 역원은 길이의 제곱으로 나눈다
lines: The general inverse is the conjugate divided by the squared norm, not the norm itself.
For [2,0,0,0], the norm is two and its square is four.
Dividing the conjugate by four gives [0.5,0,0,0].
Their product is the identity. Dividing by two would leave scalar two in the product and fail the inverse test.
For unit inputs the squared norm is one, recovering the conjugate rule.
The inverse requires a nonzero quaternion; reject zero and nonfinite inputs and inspect their origin.

scenes.title: 되돌리기에서 두 회전의 합성으로
lines: An inverse cancelled rotation. Read the red torso line separately from traveled position.
How do we connect two rotations? The next episode verifies their product.

scenes.title: 첫 편의 결과가 다음 편의 질문으로
lines: We have connected the four components to a computational representation of axis and angle, rather than four spatial directions.
Starting from a complex planar turn, we constructed a quaternion with a unit axis and half-angle, checked its norm, and verified that an inverse cancels the applied operation.
A game orientation rarely stops after one turn. The next episode explains why the order of two turns matters and calculates the extra rotation from a current orientation to a target.
